evidence.claim: A railroad bridge and tank mark the road beyond Dulce.

evidence.claim: Beyond Dulce, the road passes a railroad bridge and tank at Navajo before turning north through a canyon of rock outcrops and tall pines.
evidence.quote: travels westward through the Jicarilla Apache Nation at Dulce, and the well-preserved railroad bridge and tank at Navajo . Continuing north, rock outcrops and tall pines loom down from either side through the beautiful canyon of the Navajo River to the Colorado border.

evidence.claim: New Mexico’s tourism department describes this drive within Tracks Across Borders, a 128-mile Scenic and Historic Byway connecting Chama with Durango, Colorado.
evidence.quote: The bi-state Tracks Across Borders Scenic and Historic Byway travels 128 miles from Chama , New Mexico to Durango, Colorado.

evidence.claim: It presents the abandoned Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad right of way as the route’s historic thread.
evidence.quote: The Byway traces the historic right of way of the abandoned narrow gauge Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad, which was instrumental in the development of the region.

evidence.claim: The railroad adopted narrow gauge partly because construction and equipment cost less than standard gauge.
evidence.quote: Narrow gauge was chosen in part because construction and equipment costs would be relatively more affordable when weighed against that of the prevailing standard gauge.

evidence.claim: Most of its remaining narrow-gauge track was abandoned in the 1950s and 1960s.
evidence.quote: Most of the remaining narrow-gauge trackage was abandoned in the 1950s and 1960s.

evidence.claim: The Antonito–Chama section survived, with the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad taking over in 1970; the byway follows the abandoned corridor west of Chama.
evidence.quote: The Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad assumed operation of the line between Antonito, Colorado, and Chama, New Mexico, in 1970.

evidence.claim: For the larger journey, begin at the Cumbres and Toltec’s western terminus in Chama and head west through the Jicarilla Apache Nation at Dulce.
evidence.quote: In New Mexico, the Byway begins at the western terminus of the Cumbres and Toltec Scenic Railroad in Chama, travels westward through the Jicarilla Apache Nation at Dulce

evidence.claim: Continue past Navajo’s railroad remnants, then follow the Navajo River canyon north to the Colorado border.

evidence.claim: Dulce is the tribal headquarters of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation.
evidence.quote: It is the largest community and tribal headquarters of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation.

evidence.claim: Its ranching history begins with Jose Eugenio Gomez’s homestead in 1877.
evidence.quote: The original homestead was founded in 1877 by Jose Eugenio Gomez.

evidence.claim: The Gomez family called the ranch Agua Dulce, Spanish for sweet water, for springs that supplied people and animals with drinking water.
evidence.quote: Dulce was founded by the Gomez family as a ranching operation. The original name was "Agua Dulce," Spanish for sweet water because of the presence of natural springs that provided good drinking water for the people and their animals.

evidence.claim: A sawmill and a logging railroad later operated here, with the line extending southwest as far as Mills Lake from about 1914.
evidence.quote: A sawmill was established here, and a logging railroad running southwest as far as Mills Lake from about 1914, both of which closed around 1930.

evidence.claim: Both closed around 1930. The town remains the reservation’s largest community.
evidence.quote: A sawmill was established here, and a logging railroad running southwest as far as Mills Lake from about 1914, both of which closed around 1930.

evidence.claim: The town remains the reservation’s largest community.
evidence.quote: It is the largest community and tribal headquarters of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation.

evidence.claim: The river crosses the state boundary too: it begins in Colorado’s South San Juan Wilderness, dips into New Mexico just north of Dulce, then returns northwest to Colorado.
evidence.quote: It flows from a source in the South San Juan Wilderness of Conejos County, Colorado southwest past Chromo, Colorado. The river dips into New Mexico, passing just north of Dulce before heading northwest to a confluence with the San Juan in Archuleta County, Colorado.

evidence.claim: There it joins the San Juan River.
evidence.quote: before heading northwest to a confluence with the San Juan in Archuleta County, Colorado.

evidence.claim: A large portion of its water takes another route, diverted across the Continental Divide into the Rio Grande basin through the San Juan–Chama Project.
evidence.quote: A large portion of its water is diverted across the Continental Divide to the Rio Grande basin as part of the San Juan–Chama Project.

evidence.quote: At its height, in 1889, the D&RGW had the largest narrow-gauge railroad network in North America with 1,861 miles (2,995 km) of track interconnecting the states of Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah.

flags: The cache documents the 128-mile Tracks Across Borders corridor, not the catalog’s Narrow-Gauge name or 10.5-mile mapped segment. Omitted the current claim that the mapped road is about ten miles; overview explicitly identifies the larger journey.
Material’s strip miles run Navajo-to-Dulce, opposite the tourism narrative. Moments follow the supported reverse direction, Dulce–Navajo–river canyon; retained titles and existing coordinates.

Dulce’s cache dates the San Juan Extension through town to 1882, while the railroad history dates arrival at Durango to 1881. Omitted the local construction year; needs an authoritative railroad history to reconcile.
Navajo has only a brief tourism description. Its moment is deliberately short; no bridge dimensions, tank function, construction date or stopping/access arrangements are invented.

Current moment claims have cache support. Retained the cache’s named Gomez Ranch ownership without implying visitor access. The cache does not establish that the reservation headquarters took its name directly from the ranch; that causal phrasing is dropped.
No highway construction history, byway designation date, drive time or road-surface specification is supplied by the cache. The overview uses the documented railroad-to-byway relationship.
